newsitem.title: UK: Animal group exposes bear baiting in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Animal group exposes bear baiting in Pakistan.

text.p: An international animal protection group said on Wednesday that bear baiting was on the rise in Pakistan, despite being outlawed over 100 years ago.

Undercover agents from the World Society for the Protection of Animals (WSPA) who visited Pakistan in February discovered a resurgence of the sport in which pairs of vicious dogs attack a tethered bear. Their findings are published in a report on Wednesday called "Bear Baiting in Pakistan."

"Although bear baiting has been banned in Pakistan since 1890 and is forbidden under Islamic law, WSPA investigators were able to attend several bear baiting events," the London-based group said in a statement.
"These were well organised and attracted audiences of over 2,000 people, including children as young as five."
WSPA said up to 100 bear baiting festivals are held in Pakistan every year with about 10 bears at each event.

The bears, which have been declawed and had their teeth removed, are captured as cubs in the wild and sold to gypsies, or kalanders as they are called, for around 100 pounds ($161). Feudal landlords hold the festivals during the bear baiting season from November to April.

"Bear baiting is incredibly cruel and is based on the constant inflicting of pain on an almost totally defenceless animal. In addition, Pakistan's small and isolated populations of Asiatic brown and black bears could be wiped out if bear baiting is allowed to continued," warned WSPA investigator John Joseph, the author of the report.
The WSPA, which first exposed bear baiting in Pakistan in 1993, is urging the Pakistan government to enforce existing laws and to confiscate fighting bears.
It also wants the government to monitor the bears in the wild, to build a sanctuary for bears who have been injured, and to help the kalander communities to find alternative means of making a living.
